claims.text: As-cast or as-rolled rare-earth-free Fe-Co-Ni-Cr-based high-entropy alloys typically have heterogeneous microstructures, variable grain-boundary densities, and residual stresses.
Annealing near the magnetic ordering temperature with controlled cooling rates promotes uniform microstructural homogenization.
Greater microstructural homogeneity narrows the distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions.
Grain-boundary density and residual-stress distribution dictate the distribution of local magnetic exchange interactions.
Narrowing the distribution of exchange interactions enhances the magnetocaloric response at applied fields below 1 T.
Annealed samples will have lower magnetic hysteresis than as-cast or as-rolled controls.
Reducing magnetic inhomogeneity minimizes hysteretic losses.
Reducing microstructural and magnetic inhomogeneity facilitates rapid thermal conduction.
Annealed samples will exchange heat more rapidly than as-cast or as-rolled controls.
Controlled annealing can enhance low-field magnetocaloric performance without compromising mechanical stability.
The proposed mechanism should apply predominantly to rare-earth-free transition-metal high-entropy alloys based on elements such as Fe, Co, Ni, and Cr.
The proposed mechanism should hold specifically when processing occurs near the magnetic ordering temperature and magnetocaloric measurements use fields below 1 T.
Significant composition changes or processing parameters far outside an optimized regime may invalidate the proposed relationship.
The quantitative relationship between annealing parameters and the resulting microstructural and magnetic changes is not yet determined and may depend on subtle composition changes.
